radicals.meaningMnemonic:
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>early</radical>.

Here's a mnemonic refresher just in case: When the sun is above the cross, it's time for some people to go church — which is always way too early on a Sunday, am I right? Heck, on Sunday (日) even 10 a.m. (十)  is too early.

This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>younger brother</radical>.

Here's a mnemonic refresher just in case: There is someone wearing horns, holding a bow, and going down a slide held up by a stick. What type of person do you imagine? I'd say someone who's an immature boy. That would be your younger brother.

This looks like the helicopter radical with something extra under it. It's carrying some kind of cargo. Where's it headed? To <radical>Asia</radical>. You only know it's going to Asia because the cargo has a big TO ASIA label on it. (Go ahead and imagine it now.) 

I guess helicopters are the best way to deliver supplies in Asia because there are so many islands and mountains to fly between.

This looks like the shellfish radical, but a little different. It's the mighty <radical>crab</radical>! See the eyes and raised pincers at the top, the segmented belly in the middle, and the legs bunched up at the bottom? It takes some imagination, but this spiky shellfish definitely looks like a crab.

This looks like someone sitting with their back straight and a leg stretched out behind them. What kind of pose is this? Probably the kind you do in <radical>yoga</radical>. Sit on a yoga mat and make your body look like this radical. Nice, you're really doing yoga now.

Do you see the handles on the top and the barb on the bottom? It's a <radical>jackhammer</radical>. How can you tell? The two diagonal lines on the side show the motion of the jackhammer going up and down really fast, doing what jackhammers do. BBBHHRZHHHHRHHRZHZHHZH JUJUJUJUJU.

This radical consists of some legs carrying the sun out of prison. Those legs are yours. When the police stop you, though, what's your <radical>excuse</radical>? Come up with one and say it out loud, starting with, "My excuse is..."

This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>together</radical>. And see how it kind of looks like two people happily sitting together arm-in-arm? These two clearly enjoy doing stuff together. They're together so much they're practically joined at the hip.

Alternatively, think of this as blackjack cards held together by fins. Fish love blackjack because the hands are usually just a few cards, so even fins can hold them together.

This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>beforehand</radical>.

Here's a mnemonic refresher just in case: What does your mama tell you to do in the street? Look before you cross! You gotta do it beforehand, or it could be too late.

This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>business</radical>.

Here's a mnemonic refresher just in case: You have spikes growing out of a sheep with fins. Turn this thing into a business! You could totally charge people money to look at it. Sure, you could also donate it to science, but a business-minded person like you knows a business opportunity when you see one. Step right up! Just five dollars for a glance at the rare spiky mer-sheep!

This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>request</radical>.

Here's a mnemonic refresher just in case: Look at the ground! You spilled some water drops, so I request that you wipe them up. I'd do it myself, but you're the one who spilled them, so I'm requesting that you do it. Pretty reasonable request, right?
See the T and F that make up this radical? Those letters stand for <radical>tofu</radical>, our favorite bean curd blocks.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: People who <radical>loiter</radical> around the <radical>temple</radical> are probably just trying to <kanji>wait</kanji>. They don't mean to look like they're up to no good, but it's hard to wait without looking suspicious when you're waiting outside a temple.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine waiting outside a temple. People are giving you looks. People think you're loitering, not just waiting innocently.
kanji.readingMnemonic: As you <kanji>wait</kanji> outside the temple, you can't help but adjust your <reading>tie</reading> (たい). When you wait you get nervous, and when you get nervous you fidget. So now you're messing with your tie a whole bunch.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine adjusting your tie as you wait. Oh no, now even more people are staring at you. The tie thing is making you look even more suspicious!

kanji.meaningMnemonic: You'll have to <radical>excuse</radical> me, having all this <radical>power</radical> puts a lot of strain and <kanji>exertion</kanji> on my body. My power comes from exertion of muscle, so please excuse me if I start to perspire.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine yourself under great exertion. You're attempting to use your power to move something and it's really requiring a lot of exertion to move. Picture yourself doing this action and imagine how difficult it is.
kanji.readingMnemonic: That thing you're moving that requires such incredible <kanji>exertion</kanji> is a <reading>ben</reading>to (べん). It's a massive bento box full of the heaviest foods. Why did you make a bento that requires so much exertion to move? Kinda defeats the purpose of a bento.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine a bento box the size of a truck. It's full of heavy foods, like rice and and fried stuff, and cheese… Takes exertion to move this bento, and exertion to digest it.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: There's a <radical>canopy</radical> and a man called the <radical>Yoga</radical> <radical>King</radical> standing in the middle of your <kanji>garden</kanji>.
kanji.meaningHint: Somehow your little garden is now being used by the Yoga King to teach yoga to a whole group of random people under this canopy... you have no idea how they got back here.
kanji.readingMnemonic: Not only is this Yoga King taking over your <kanji>garden</kanji>, but he's ordering you to serve food to his class. "You there, peasant, fetch these people your freshest <reading>ta</reading>ter (てい) tots from this puny garden to give them strength."
kanji.readingHint: You're not sure what else to do, so you end up serving tater tots in your garden all day to stretchy strangers.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: Imagining one’s <radical>self</radical> without a <radical>heart</radical> can make it hard to draw <kanji>breath</kanji>. Without a heart, you’d have no blood pumping and you would start to die. This would make it increasingly harder to draw breath and get oxygen to stay alive.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine trying to live without a heart. You couldn’t. Your blood stops flowing and your body shuts down. You would no longer be able to draw breath.
kanji.readingMnemonic: You know how when people are unconscious and their <kanji>breath</kanji> slows or comes to a stop, they use smelling salts to revive them? Well a smelly <reading>sock</reading> (そく) can work just as well. Socks get really stinky and their stench is powerful enough to revive someone who isn’t drawing breath.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine smelling this smelly sock. Imagine the smelly stench of the dirty sock wafting up into your nostrils and filling your lungs with its odor. Gross.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>direction</radical> your <radical>gun</radical> is facing leads straight to a block of <radical>tofu</radical>. This might be a sign you need to take a <kanji>trip</kanji>. If you're out there pointing guns at tofu, you're probably a little… tired… and in need of a change of scenery. Take a trip!
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine coming to your senses after shooting up a block of tofu for stress relief or whatever you were doing. Yeah, you gotta get away from tofu for a while… It's definitely time for a relaxing trip.
kanji.readingMnemonic: So, where do you go on your <kanji>trip</kanji>? To <reading>Rio</reading> (りょ). You had to go way down south to get as far away as possible from tofu. Ahh, nothing like a nice trip to Rio!
kanji.readingHint: Imagine soaking up the sun on the beaches of Rio de Janeiro. Rio has its fair share of guns, but at least there's a lot less tofu around these parts.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: A <radical>tree</radical> <radical>root</radical> is still just a <kanji>root</kanji>!
kanji.meaningHint: Roots are roots, ね.
kanji.readingMnemonic: Tree <kanji>root</kanji>s are the perfect roosting place for <reading>con</reading>dors (こん). Unfortunately, living on roots is also why they're always endangered. Condors can be killed pretty easily living on the ground on roots like this.
kanji.readingHint: Picture a family of condors nestled at the bottom of a tree in its roots. Then a huge machine comes over and mows them all down as it cuts all the trees off their roots. Darn you humans! Do you have to ruin everything?!

kanji.meaningMnemonic: A <radical>tsunami</radical> lifts all the <radical>trash</radical> out of the <radical>river</radical> and it <kanji>stream</kanji>s out onto the shores.
kanji.meaningHint: As the tsunami recedes, watch as all of the trash comes streaming out of the river and crowds the bank.
kanji.readingMnemonic: Next to the trash <kanji>stream</kanji> you suddenly see <reading>Ryu</reading> (りゅう) from Street Fighter and he looks pissed. He's furious that so many people throw their trash in the river and it causes streams like this.
kanji.readingHint: Now Ryu is punching and kicking and tatsumaki senpukyaku-ing all of the trash into burnable and non-burnable piles. But the stream doesn't end. Now he's trying to get his other Street Fighter pals to help him beat it back!

kanji.meaningMnemonic: A long time ago a huge <radical>tsunami</radical> swept a <radical>triceratops</radical> up into the <radical>moon</radical> and <kanji>extinguish</kanji>ed its life.
kanji.meaningHint: I’m sure you’ve heard many theories on how dinosaurs went extinct. Well, this is the real story. Imagine this poor triceratops and all his friends being extinguished by this powerful tsunami, sweeping them up into the moon where there's no air to breathe or leaves to eat.
kanji.readingMnemonic: This famous event where almost all life was <kanji>extinguish</kanji>ed is reenacted every year for the <reading>Shou</reading>gun (しょう). He's got a bit of an unhealthy obsession with extinguishing life...
kanji.readingHint: Watch the Shougun's eyes light up as an actor dressed like a tsunami crashes into an actor dressed as a triceratops and all of the lights on the stage are extinguished. Spooky...

kanji.meaningMnemonic:
A <radical>leader</radical> who hires his own personal <radical>clown</radical> will likely <kanji>double</kanji> his entertainment. Clowns are funny and make people laugh, so the leader decided to hire one. Since that time, the leader's amount of mirth has doubled. 

This also means <kanji>times</kanji>, which makes sense when you think about the kind of math you'll need to double something. What is A * 2? It's A doubled, first of all, but you're using multiplication. You're "timesing" something.
kanji.meaningHint: Picture a clown and all the ridiculous funny things they do. Imagine the clown throwing a pie at someone's face and how funny that is. Chuckle to yourself and remember this kanji.
kanji.readingMnemonic: When the clown stops being funny, it's time to say <reading>bye</reading> (ばい). At first, the clown <kanji>double</kanji>d the leader's entertainment, but now the clown is just annoying. It's time to say bye-bye.
kanji.readingHint: This clown has served its purpose. Wave your hand in the air and say bye-bye to this worthless clown.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: Even a <radical>mouth</radical>-bearing <radical>shellfish</radical> is a <kanji>member</kanji> of the invertebrate family. Yes, shellfish do have mouths, look it up!
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine a shellfish opening and closing its mouth, talking to you and telling you what a proud member of its family it is. It's a strange sight, but picture it in your mind anyway.
kanji.readingMnemonic: If you were a <kanji>member</kanji> of the same shellfish family, you'd be able to go to the special shellfish <reading>inn</reading> (いん). Every species has a members-only inn.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine trying to go to the shellfish inn. Imagine all the members-only signs telling you that you can't come in. Womp womp.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: A <radical>bird</radical> sits upon a <radical>mountain</radical>. If you look at the radicals, the bird is quite large and the mountain quite small. Think of this in the mnemonic as well. The reason the mountain is small is because you can only see the top of it, sticking out of the water. On it is the bird. This small mountain with the bird on it is an <kanji>island</kanji>.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine the mountain as small as you'd like. Maybe it's only barely sticking out of the sea, and the bird is having trouble standing on it. Whatever you do, make sure you think of it as an island, possibly owned by the bird.
kanji.readingMnemonic: But this <kanji>island</kanji> doesn't only belong to the bird. In fact, the bird shouldn't be on this island, because it belongs to the <reading>She</reading>ep <reading>Ma</reading>ma (しま), who is like Mother Nature but for sheep. The all-powerful Sheep Mama comes to kick the bird off the island, because this place is only for sheep! All hail the Sheep Mama.
kanji.readingHint: The Sheep Mama is a huge, majestic sheep with magical powers. She kicks the bird off the island with her hooves, and the bird squawks and flies away as fast as it can.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>moon</radical> shines down on a <radical>stool</radical> and a <radical>jackhammer</radical> which are there for the upcoming <kanji>festival</kanji>. Festivals need activities, and at this festival, you can sit on a stool in the moonlight and use a jackhammer to make a lot of noise. Perfect for a festival!
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine being at a moonlit festival and waiting in line for the stool and jackhammer. You don't want to eat candy apples or ride rides, you want to wait your turn to try out the jackhammer (while comfortably seated on a stool, of course).
kanji.readingMnemonic: This <kanji>festival</kanji> is for <reading>cy</reading>borgs (さい) only. Picture the cyborg you made getting excited that you're taking it to the festival. That's why all of the activities have to do with heavy machinery. The rides are mostly just cyborgs letting other people ride them, but it's still pretty fun.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine your cyborg going to this festival. Everyone here has some type of cyborg enhancement, like robotic arms, legs, or braces. Your cyborg is really excited to be around its people and play with jackhammers.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: You <radical>stand</radical> at a podium <radical>early</radical> in the morning to practice reading the <kanji>chapter</kanji> from your latest book.
kanji.meaningHint: Picture yourself, standing tall in the light of the early morning. You hold your head up high, open to your bookmark, and read the name of the chapter aloud: "Chapter 42: The Most Important Number."
kanji.readingMnemonic: You're practicing this specific <kanji>chapter</kanji> because you've been asked to read it for the <reading>Shou</reading>gun (しょう). There will be a bunch of other authors reading chapters of their books to him too, and you want to make a good impression.
kanji.readingHint: Picture yourself in a line with other authors, standing in the early morning, waiting to read chapters from your respective books. You really hope the Shougun likes yours. If he does, you'll be famous! If he doesn't, you might be beheaded.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: <radical>Bamboo</radical>'s <radical>younger brother</radical> is counted with an <kanji>ordinal number prefix</kanji>. An ordinal number is one that represents a position or rank in sequential order (like first, second, third, etc.). We use this ordinal number prefix before counting these things in Japanese sometimes. Like with bamboo, going down in order toward the youngest.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine a line of bamboo shoots arranged from oldest to youngest. They look like pipe organ pipes, or a xylophone, and now you need to count them.
kanji.readingMnemonic: To remember you need to use the <kanji>ordinal number prefix</kanji> before you count these bamboo, you <reading>dye</reading> (だい) them.
kanji.readingHint: Now they're in descending order already, and you can count them nice and easy thanks to your dye method.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: <radical>Someone</radical>s and <radical>building</radical>s, someones and buildings, someones and buildings. So many someones and buildings. With so many someones and buildings, we have ourselves a <kanji>metropolis</kanji>.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine just a ton of someones and buildings all packed together in a small area. More than a village or town or city. With enough someones and buildings, you end up with a metropolis.
kanji.readingMnemonic: In this <kanji>metropolis</kanji> everything is a <reading>toe</reading> (と). The someones are toes, walking around. The buildings are toes, too.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine this huge metropolis. Now imagine every building just being a toe. Tall skyscraper toes. Smaller house toes. Wide apartment building toes. And then the people walking around. They are toes, too. Toes walking around and going into toe buildings, with toe cars and toe dogs. If you imagine the toe metropolis deeply enough, it should be weird enough to burn into your memory.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: When something is <radical>heavy</radical>, you need a lot of <radical>power</radical> to <kanji>move</kanji> it. It’s not going to move unless you use a lot of power. That thing is heavy and unless you use all the power you got, it’s not moving.
kanji.meaningHint: Picture a massive 1 ton weight. It’s heavy. You can’t even begin to move it without some sort of powerful machine to help you. Imagine yourself trying to move it with just your bare hands.
kanji.readingMnemonic: Remember that 1 ton weight? Well, actually it’s a <reading>dou</reading>ghnut (どう). A huge, massive, 1 ton doughnut. It’s super heavy and hard to move, but it’s delicious.
kanji.readingHint: Okay, so you don’t have enough power to move this doughnut as is. In order to move it, you’re going to have to use your superhuman power of eating. Once you eat enough of it, the remainder will be easy to move. Imagine yourself digging into this massive doughnut and taste its fresh baked goodness on your tongue. It’s mighty tasty.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: A <radical>stand</radical>ing <radical>mustache</radical> with <radical>legs</radical> is able to sell <kanji>merchandise</kanji>. Most mustaches can’t stand because they don’t have legs. This mustache, however, does. It also has a keen business sense, which is why it’s selling merchandise.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine this mustache entrepreneur, standing at his merchandise stand, selling his wares. He looks quite dignified, legs and all.
kanji.readingMnemonic: The mustache is selling his <kanji>merchandise</kanji> so well that even the <reading>Shou</reading>gun (しょう) notices. He leans down really close to the standing mustache man's merchandise and stays very still. Then he snaps his fingers and his servants come rushing out to buy it all!
kanji.readingHint: Now all of the merchandise belongs to the Shougun. The mustache has nothing left to sell, but at least he's rich!

kanji.meaningMnemonic: In <radical>Asia</radical> they assume everyone's <radical>heart</radical> is automatically <kanji>bad</kanji> and <kanji>evil</kanji>.
kanji.meaningHint: You don't want a bunch of evil in your heart, do you? No, I didn't think so.
kanji.readingMnemonic: Luckily, people in Asia know how to get the <kanji>evil</kanji> <kanji>bad</kanji>ness out of your heart with <reading>acu</reading>puncture (あく).
kanji.readingHint: Acupuncture was originally invented in Asia a long, long time ago, to stop the bad chi from going through your heart.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: If someone is headed in your <radical>direction</radical> with a <radical>gun</radical>, nock an <radical>arrow</radical> in your bow and gather your <kanji>tribe</kanji> behind you because it’s about to get real! This man with a gun is headed your direction and he doesn’t even know what you and your tribe are gonna do to him. If he gets any closer, you’re likely to shoot that arrow right at him.
kanji.meaningHint: This guy headed your direction with his gun doesn’t look friendly at all. Hear the sound of the bowstring as you nock your arrow and prepare your shot to defend yourself. Then imagine the sound of everyone in your tribe doing the same.
kanji.readingMnemonic: When he starts to get closer, you notice that this guy is a boso<reading>zoku</reading> (ぞく) bike gang member. Bosozoku means “running <kanji>tribe</kanji>” and this guy is running right at you. With a gun. So gather your own tribe behind you and prepare to defend yourself against this bosozoku member.
kanji.readingHint: You remember what a bosozoku is, right? We wrote about them on Tofugu a while ago. They’re bike gang members and the “zoku” in bosozoku means tribe. Remember that article when you see this kanji.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: If a <radical>tsunami</radical> is higher than your <radical>forehead</radical> you better move those <radical>legs</radical> and find a <radical>tree</radical> to climb, because that thing is <kanji>deep</kanji>!
kanji.meaningHint: Picture this tsunami rushing past the tree you managed to climb up. It's a deep one, way higher than your forehead, but you're safe here. Legs exhausted, sure, but safe and sound.
kanji.readingMnemonic: You wait until the tsunami is only as <kanji>deep</kanji> as your <reading>shin</reading> (しん). Then you climb down the tree and wade home in the shin-deep water.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine all the debris floating in the shin-deep water now, bumping up against your shins. Probably hurts, considering how sensitive shins are.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>king</radical> <radical>request</radical>s a <kanji>sphere</kanji>!
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine the king holding a sphere in his hand, and looking at it. It's a green sphere, and that is because...
kanji.readingMnemonic: The <kanji>sphere</kanji> is a <reading>cu</reading>cumber (きゅう) sphere. A strange sphere shaped cucumber.
kanji.readingHint: Now imagine the king requesting a cucumber sphere, and holding it up to look at it. If you want, have him take a bite out of the sphere, and say "this sphere is a cucumber?" Imagine the taste of it. Imagine the smell, and its bumpy cucumber skin.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: Those who <radical>stand</radical> on top of a <radical>village</radical> are <kanji>juvenile</kanji>. Imagine a bunch of young people standing on the roofs of buildings in the village. That's a juvenile thing to do.
kanji.meaningHint: Picture all those juveniles standing on top of buildings in your village, being bored, and doing juvenile things.
kanji.readingMnemonic: Mostly, though, the  <kanji>juvenile</kanji>s are standing on top of village buildings, eating <reading>dou</reading>ghnuts (どう).
kanji.readingHint: Imagine looking up to the top of the buildings in your village. Thousands of juveniles, staring down at you and everyone else, eating doughnuts. The crumbs falling down on top of you. But, the doughnuts smell good, at least. Maybe you try to catch some crumbs.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: Look at a <radical>building</radical> and <radical>compare</radical> the <radical>white</radical> parts. Each of those white parts is a <kanji>floor</kanji>. Multi-<kanji>story</kanji> buildings have tons of different floors that you can see from the outside.
kanji.meaningHint: All buildings have white marks that you can compare with the rest to see where the floors are.
kanji.readingMnemonic: One <kanji>floor</kanji> is just all <reading>kay</reading>aks (かい). You're looking at this building, and every other <kanji>story</kanji> is normal, but that one floor is kayak after kayak after kayak.
kanji.readingHint: Kayaks working at desks. Kayaks that are desks. Kayaks walking around checking on other kayaks. The kayak floor is quite odd. It's odd there is a floor only about kayaks.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>roof</radical>, even though it's almost <radical>spring</radical>, is still covered in <radical>ice</radical> so it's <kanji>cold</kanji>. Inside the house is cold, outside the house is cold. Everything is cold!
kanji.meaningHint: Picture the entire roof covered in ice. It's supposed to be spring right now, but it's too cold for the ice to melt off your roof.
kanji.readingMnemonic: You can't stand the <kanji>cold</kanji> anymore, so you hire a <reading>samu</reading>rai (さむ) to come try to hack the ice off of your roof with his sword. You stand outside shivering, and watching as the samurai tries to stab the ice off of your roof.
kanji.readingHint: The samurai isn't doing a good job stopping the cold, and soon he and his sword have frozen into your ice roof. So now it's cold and you have a dead samurai stuck to your house. Great.

kanji.meaningMnemonic:
If the <radical>sun</radical> is on <radical>someone</radical>, they will get <kanji>hot</kanji>. That's just how it is. Someone standing out in the sun for a long time will inevitably get hot. The sun is hot, and it makes you get hot too.

Note that this usually refers to hot weather or the heat of an area you're in and doesn't refer to a hot "thing."
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine you're this someone, standing out in the hot sun. Feel the hot rays beating down on you. You're getting all sweaty and sticky from the heat now, ugh.
kanji.readingMnemonic: One sun was <kanji>hot</kanji> enough, but then a second one shows up. "<reading>Ah, two</reading> (あつ)!" you scream. If you were sweaty and sticky from the heat of just one sun, imagine what this second one is going to do to you. Ah, two hot suns!
kanji.readingHint: Feel the hot rays of sunlight beating down on you from two directions. "Ah, two hot suns is more than I can take," you gasp as your body slowly melts into a human puddle of sweat.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: A "<radical>crab</radical> <radical>moon</radical>" is a specific <kanji>period of time</kanji>.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine looking at the moon and seeing a crab on it and thinking: "oh, it's the crab moon <kanji>time period</kanji>."
kanji.readingMnemonic: When the crab moon <kanji>period of time</kanji> is upon us, we must take a special <reading>key</reading> (き) and lock everything in such a way that crabs cannot get in.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine a key with a little crab moon on it, denoting the Crab Moon period of time. Then, go around and lock everything with it and watch thousands of crabs trying to get into everything. Luckily, they can't, because you have a special key that locks things so crabs can't get in. When the Crab Moon time period is over, you can use your key to unlock everything.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: If you want a <radical>tree</radical> to grow <radical>straight</radical>, you have to <kanji>plant</kanji> it properly. Everyone knows that poorly planted trees grow all crooked and twisted. That's just how plants work. If your tree's not straight, start over and plant it again.
kanji.meaningHint: After four or five attempts, you've finally planted a perfectly straight tree. Pat yourself on the back for a job well done.
kanji.readingMnemonic: You <kanji>plant</kanji> and re-plant your tree over and over, utterly <reading>shock</reading>ed (しょく) at how hard it is to plant it right. You thought planting trees was easy, so this is a real shock to you.
kanji.readingHint: After planting your tree and failing again for the 100th time, you stand there in total shock. How could it be this difficult?

kanji.meaningMnemonic: <radical>Stop</radical>! That <radical>box</radical> of <radical>rice</radical> is actually full of <kanji>teeth</kanji>! I know it says "rice" on the cover, but I promise you those are all teeth and if you bite into them you'll break a <kanji>tooth</kanji> of your own.
kanji.meaningHint: Stop what you're doing and look into the rice box. Nope, it's definitely full of teeth. There's a grain or two of rice, but it's like 98% teeth.
kanji.readingMnemonic: Why do I have a rice box full of <kanji>teeth</kanji>? <reading>Hah</reading> (は)! Wouldn't you like to know. Hah! I definitely have an answer that isn't weird or creepy…
kanji.readingHint: On second thought, I don't need to explain my box of teeth to you. Hah! Figure it out yourself.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: There's a <radical>tsunami</radical> which washes a <radical>plate</radical> out into the <radical>sun</radical>. Because it's in the sun, it becomes  <kanji>warm</kanji>.
kanji.meaningHint: Right after the tsunami, this plate was wet, but the sun is warming and drying the plate. Imagine looking at the plate and seeing the beads of water evaporate off it as it warms up. Feel the warm steam on your face as this happens.
kanji.readingMnemonic: The plate starts to get so <kanji>warm</kanji> that you could fry an <reading>on</reading>ion (おん) on it. Who doesn’t love fried onions? That plate sure is warm enough, so start cookin’ ‘em!
kanji.readingHint: Imagine yourself frying onions on this plate warmed by the sun. Smell the onion smell as the onion fumes get into your eyes and your sinuses. It makes your eyes water as you are very sensitive to onions.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: There's a <radical>tsunami</radical> coming and you want to be <radical>together</radical> with it by <radical>yourself</radical> (oneself) so you go to the <kanji>harbor</kanji>.
kanji.meaningHint: Picture the harbor. You're the only one there. The wind is whipping violently and all of the boats docked around you are being bounced around. You can see the tsunami rising out of the ocean and coming for you and the harbor.
kanji.readingMnemonic: As you look around at the <kanji>harbor</kanji> in your last moments you suddenly see someone in the water. It's <reading>こう</reading>いち! He's sitting in an inner tube in the harbor waiting for the tsunami too.
kanji.readingHint: Well this sucks. You wanted to enjoy being alone together with the tsunami and the harbor, but now こういち is here ruining your peace. He's floating around in the harbor like everything isn't about to be destroyed, sipping on a fancy drink in his inner tube.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: If there's a <radical>tsunami</radical> it's <radical>easy</radical> to get <kanji>hot water</kanji>. Just stick your hand out the window as the tsunami goes by and poof! That water's HOT.
kanji.meaningHint: Picture the boiling hot tsunami water as it comes for you. Psh, this will be easy.
kanji.readingMnemonic: As the <kanji>hot water</kanji> comes, you just lift up the bottom of the <reading>yu</reading>rt (ゆ) you live in, and it comes flowing in. All of the cups, pots, and barrels you laid on your floor are now full of hot water.
kanji.readingHint: You decided to live in a yurt because of the easy access it provides to hot water. They're so mobile!

kanji.meaningMnemonic: There's a <radical>tent</radical> of <radical>beans</radical>. You try to <kanji>climb</kanji> it.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine this tent of beans. Make it huge, bulging with beans! Now, get climbing. Feel the beans on the other side of the tent's wall.
kanji.readingMnemonic: You <kanji>climb</kanji> the bean tent, and from this vantage point you can see <reading>とう</reading>きょう in the distance.
kanji.readingHint: It's beautiful! It's breathtaking! All your climbing makes this view of とうきょう even more worthwhile!

kanji.meaningMnemonic: A <radical>horn</radical>ed <radical>king</radical> on a <radical>slide</radical> catches your <radical>eye</radical> because you love what he's chosen to <kanji>wear</kanji>. You can't wait for him to <kanji>arrive</kanji> at the bottom of the slide so you can check out his outfit close-up.
kanji.meaningHint: Try to picture what this king is wearing as he comes down the slide and arrives at the bottom. He can surely afford to wear the finest garments — plus, his horns give him all sorts of options for accessorizing.
kanji.readingMnemonic: How does this king decide what to <kanji>wear</kanji> each day? He uses <reading>chalk</reading> (ちゃく) to sketch out his wardrobe ideas on a chalkboard. This helps him <kanji>arrive</kanji> at a conclusion faster.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine the sound of horrible chalk squeaks as the king furiously sketches all sorts of crazy outfits on his massive royal chalkboard — all the while muttering "What to wear, what to wear?"

kanji.meaningMnemonic: If you use an <radical>arrow</radical> to shoot a stalk of <radical>beans</radical>, the bean plant will end up <kanji>short</kanji>. When the beans are hit with that arrow, it severs the plant in two, and you are left with a stalk of beans that is much shorter than before.
kanji.meaningHint: Picture yourself shooting this arrow. Imagine yourself nocking the arrow to the bow, and pulling the string back. That bean plant is not short enough, and you're going to do something about it.
kanji.readingMnemonic: All this shooting of arrows to make the bean plants <kanji>short</kanji> is taking a long time. Since you're out in the sun, you're starting to get a <reading>tan</reading> (たん). After the day is finally over, your tan is really, really dark.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine yourself being out in the sun for so long that you get an amazing tan. Your skin feels warm all over from all the sun you were getting throughout the day. Feel the warmth coming off of your tanned skin.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>village</radical> <radical>beforehand</radical> (what the village was before it was a village) was a <kanji>field</kanji>.
kanji.meaningHint: It makes sense for a big open field to have been what was there before the village was made.
kanji.readingMnemonic: On this <kanji>field</kanji>, the <reading>Ya</reading>nkees (や) used to play.
kanji.readingHint: It was sad that they had to destroy the natural habitat of the Yankees (a field) to put up the village.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: <radical>White</radical> <radical>water</radical> shoots out from a <kanji>spring</kanji> in the ground. Due to the force the water shoots from the spring, the water looks white with all the air bubbles.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine these geysers and the white water shooting from the springs under the ground. Now imagine yourself standing over one when the water shoots out. You’d get super wet and probably knocked over due to the force of the spring water. Imagine this happening to yourself.
kanji.readingMnemonic: From the <kanji>spring</kanji>, a <reading>cen</reading>taur (せん) emerges.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine this centaur pushing its way out from the hole in the ground, plugging the water as it squeezes through the hole. Why was there a centaur in the spring? Once it gets out, imagine the centaur standing in front of the spring as it bubbles up and starts shooting water out again. This spring belongs to the centaur.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The radical <radical>suit</radical> and the kanji <kanji>suit</kanji> are exactly the same! This kanji can also mean <kanji>join</kanji> which makes sense. When something suits you well, like a hat or something, it joins together with you quite well too. Join me, my hat! You suit my head well. It just <kanji>fit</kanji>s, you know?
kanji.meaningHint: Just remember that this "suit" means "to suit you" - not the thing you wear, okay!
kanji.readingMnemonic:
You need someone who will <kanji>suit</kanji> you. Someone who can <kanji>join</kanji> you on your life journey. So you call Grandpa <reading>ごう</reading>いち.

Note: For the ごう reading mnemonics, we use Grandpa ごういち because こういち is used for the こう reading. So just remember that ごう comes from Koichi's grandpa ごういち.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine you two standing next to each other, posing for a photograph. You two suit each other well. Grandpa ごういち with his gray beard, and you with your [well, you have to fill in this part by yourself].

kanji.meaningMnemonic: If you <radical>loiter</radical> around my <radical>skin</radical>, <kanji>he</kanji> will get angry at you. He's my very protective friend, and you don't wanna make him angry!
kanji.meaningHint: He's already eyeing you down, loitering this close to my skin. Might wanna... back up a little.
kanji.readingMnemonic: <kanji>He</kanji> may get grumpy if you loiter around my skin, but a well-made <reading>curry</reading> (かれ) always brightens his mood. So give him some curry.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine him turning from a frown to a broad smile as he smells the fragrant curry you've brought.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: A <radical>leader</radical> of <radical>business</radical>? Ha! That's <kanji>me</kanji>! That's <kanji>I</kanji>!
kanji.meaningHint: This version of <kanji>I</kanji> is more boyish. It's a sort of young man/boy way of saying "I," though you'll hear women use it too sometimes (it's a teensy bit tomboyish though).
kanji.readingMnemonic: You use the word <kanji>I</kanji> a lot. You say it so much, you just start referring to yourself with the french <reading>beaucoup</reading> (ぼく) for a lot. Because you love yourself a lot.
kanji.readingHint: I am beaucoup I am. (Is that a pun? Did I do it right?) I dunno. Just say ぼく a lot and try to connect all of your approximate knowledges of languages together. Merci ぼく from ぼく.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: I have <radical>sick</radical> in my <radical>skin</radical>. Just look at it, it doesn't look too good. Whenever I have sickness in my skin, I know that I'm probably <kanji>tired</kanji>.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine yourself being really, really tired. Then look at your skin. It's all blotchy and sickly looking.
kanji.readingMnemonic: Why so <kanji>tired</kanji>? Your body is <reading>hea</reading>ted (ひ) up from exercising way too much. You should let that heat cool down so your skin starts looking better.
kanji.readingHint: Feel all the heat (ひ) emanating from your body. It makes you realize how very, very tired you are.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: This word has the kanji for <kanji>one</kanji> and <kanji>era</kanji>. You only have one era to live in, so this is the only <vocabulary>lifetime</vocabulary> you get. Unless you're reborn, but that will probably be in the next era, not this one. So one lifetime for you!

You find it quite handy <vocabulary>to use</vocabulary> <reading>two car</reading>s (つか) in your daily life. The big minivan? You use that for grocery shopping and taking the kids to soccer practice. vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means start, and this verb means to begin or to start. 始まる is the intransitive version, so it doesn't take a direct object. A war begins, for example, or the new school term starts. No direct object, right? Verbs ending in okurigana that rhyme with ある tend to be intransitive like this. You can remember this because if something is ある, it's just there, existing, not acting on anything else. That's why verbs that sound like it are often intransitive too!
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading.

Lucky for you, the kanji readings for transitive and intransitive verbs are almost always the same. Once you learn one, you know them both! This reading is the same as 始める.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>chirp</kanji> <kanji>voice</kanji> is a sound an animal makes. Sure, it works for birds (which chirp), but it also works with most other animals as well. So, we call this an <vocabulary>animal cry</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The readings are those that you learned with the kanji. 声 gets changed to ごえ, though, so take note of that in your head. Perhaps you can imagine an animal that does a "GOEEEEE" cry.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: A <kanji>thing</kanji> you <kanji>drink</kanji> is a <vocabulary>beverage</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: These are both the kun'yomi readings. You've learned them already, so you already know how to read this word!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
You've seen 聞く by now hopefully. This is similar, but instead of meaning "to hear" it means <vocabulary>to be hearable</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be audible</vocabulary>. To remember this, just think about how you can hear a こえ (voice) coming from the middle of the word 聞こえる. It's audible to you too, right?

聞こえる is used when sounds reach your ears on their own, like "I can hear music from next door." It's more about what comes to your ears, not what you're trying to listen to. That's why it also means <vocabulary>to be able to hear</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading comes from 聞く, so if you know the reading of that word, you can apply it here.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: Remember how 心配 means "a worry" and 事 can mean "thing"? Well, if you have a worry over some specific thing, then you probably have some <vocabulary>cares</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>worries</vocabulary>. What are your 心配事 these days?
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading is the reading of 心配 (which you've hopefully gotten down okay by now) and 事 using the (こと) reading. It is rendaku'd, as well, so beware of the ごと. (Just another 心配事, am I right?)

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>sound</kanji> <kanji>read</kanji>ing. What could this be...? Wait a sec, think to Japanese and kanji. What's the reading that uses sounds from another place, specifically China? That's the <vocabulary>Chinese reading</vocabulary>, aka the <vocabulary>on'yomi</vocabulary>. Sounds familiar?
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading for 音 is the 音読み. 読み uses the kun'yomi, though, strangely. Way to mess up the one word that should be all on'yomi, Japan. Way. To. Go.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: You know that <vocabulary>運転</vocabulary> has to do with driving, right? And you know that <kanji>手</kanji> often has to do with a person doing something in words like these. So, a person who does driving is what? A <vocabulary>driver</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading is all on'yomi, because it's jukugo. You should know the on'yomi reading of 手 by now just by seeing similar word patterns to this one.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>leaf</kanji> that <kanji>fall</kanji>s are <vocabulary>fallen leaves</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading for this one is a bit strange. You'll have to pull from your knowledge of 落ちる and use that for the first half. Then, 葉 is rendaku'd to ば. Because, when a leaf falls, Scrooge says "BAH! Humbug!" (probably because he's losing money).

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: Your <kanji>father</kanji> <kanji>parent</kanji> is your <vocabulary>father</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading here is pretty weird. It's all kun'yomi. My guess is this translates literally to "father parent" (two different words, therefore uses the other readings). You should know the readings of these two separate words, though. It is 父 (ちち) and 親 (おや).

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>mother</kanji> <kanji>parent</kanji> is the <vocabulary>mother</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading for this is strange. It's the kun'yomi vocab reading, probably because the literal translation is "mother parent" and therefore consists of a couple words combined together into one concept. So, make sure you know the separate word readings of 母 and 親. If you do, you should be able to read this too.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
Remember 一番目? This is just like that, but with three, making it <vocabulary>the third thing</vocabulary> or simply <vocabulary>the third</vocabulary>.

Again, think about your eyeball collection. This time, you're showing someone the third eyeball in your display case. It just happens to be third in line, but honestly it's just as beautiful as the two that come before it.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: Use your knowledge of the reading for 一番目 to remember the reading for this word as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: Since 話す means "to speak," your <kanji>way</kanji> of doing that would be your <vocabulary>way of speaking</vocabulary> or your <vocabulary>speaking style</vocabulary>. This includes your tone of voice, speed, and even how you use gestures when talking. It's more about the whole way you communicate, not just the wording or how you phrase things.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This word uses kun'yomi readings for both kanji. You learned the はな reading with 話す, and the かた reading for 方 is the one you learned with other "how-to" words like 言い方 (how to say) and 読み方 (how to read).

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: Do you remember the word 転がる? This is kind of similar, instead of rolling, this is more for when something falls and hits the ground. It means <vocabulary>to fall over</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to fall down</vocabulary>. Just imagine someone falling off a chair face first into the dirt and making a ぶ sound.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading comes from 転がる. Hopefully you know that one well enough to associate it with this one, meaning you can read them both.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: I bet you remember 集める means "to collect something." But this time you're not collecting something. Instead, something just… collects. In other words, 集まる means to come together or to gather. Friends come together, or fans gather at a venue — that sort of thing. No direct object needed, since this is intransitive. Verbs ending in okurigana that rhyme with ある tend to be intransitive like this. You can remember this because if something is ある, it's just there, existing, not acting on anything else. That's why verbs that sound like it are often intransitive too!
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as 集める so if you know that word you'll know how to read this word as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: You've seen how 落ちる means "to fall down." Now you're doing the action of "falling something down," aka you're dropping it. You can remember this because you kind of <reading>toss</reading> (とす) something and it drops to the ground, making this word mean <vocabulary>to drop something</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading comes from 落ちる. So long as you know that word you can apply that reading over here, too.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: By now you should know that 終わる means "to end" or "to finish." So what is this noun-version of that word? It would be <vocabulary>the end</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>the finish</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading comes from 終わる. So long as you know that word, you can learn this word's reading as well!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: We've seen a few times where 電 refers to a train. They're big deals, after all, and use a ton of electricity. So, the <kanji>end</kanji> train for this word would refer to the <vocabulary>last train</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: You should know 開ける by now. This word is similar to that, except it has to do with when things are just open. It's the same thing, though. The meaning is also <vocabulary>to open</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
Do you remember the reading for 開ける, which you learned in level 10? That's right, it's あける! So if you know the reading of that word (I hope you do!) then you can apply that knowledge here.

Just a quick side note — 開く can also be read as ひらく, but we're going to focus on the あく reading here. Since ひらく has slightly different meanings, we won't accept it as a reading for this word, so be sure to enter あく!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: You know that 起きる means "to wake up", but did you learn its secondary meaning, "to occur"? Well, this word means only <vocabulary>to occur</vocabulary>. Just imagine an incident occurring involving a uranium <reading>core</reading> (こる) to remember that this means <vocabulary>to occur</vocabulary>. After all, uranium core incidents don't wake up, do they?
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as what you learned with the kanji and the same as 起きる too, meaning you should be able to put together the reading on your own.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: You know that 心配 is "a worry." What about the verb version of that? It would be <vocabulary>to worry</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading comes straight from 心配 so try to make sure you know that word so you can read this word! It's also all jukugo on'yomi reading, too, so you should be able to figure it out regardless.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: You learned 鳴く means "to chirp" (or some other animal sound). 鳴る is similar, but it's used when something just makes a sound, like a phone ringing, a bell jingling, or thunder rumbling. So 鳴る means <vocabulary>to sound</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to ring</vocabulary>. You know this because 鳴る can also be used for when your stomach rumbles: "<reading>rrrr</reading>" (る)!
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading can come from 鳴く. So long as you know the reading for that word you can know the reading for this word as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. One of the kanji's meanings is <kanji>sing</kanji> so the verb vocab version of this is <vocabulary>to sing</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: Awesomely, this uses the same reading as the reading for the vocab words 歌. Just throw the う onto the end and you have yourself the reading. So, sing your heart out and learn this word easily. "IIIIiiIIIiiiII WILLL ALLllwaYYYs Loovvve YoOooOOooooOOOO ♬!"

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>hand</kanji> (or person, as you know 手 often refers to a person) that <kanji>win</kanji>s gets to do <vocabulary>as one pleases</vocabulary> without regard for anyone else.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading for this is weird. It's all kun'yomi, which luckily you've seen before, but still strange. I guess when you do <vocabulary>as one pleases</vocabulary> you can read kanji however you want, in this case the kun'yomi readings. Do note that there's a small っ in there before 手, presumably to connect the two readings of the two kanji together.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji means transmit, and this verb version is to be transmitted or to be conveyed. It's intransitive, so it doesn't take a direct object. A message is transmitted, or your feelings are conveyed — that kind of thing. Verbs ending in okurigana that rhyme with ある tend to be intransitive like this. You can remember this because if something is ある, it's just there, existing, not acting on anything else. That's why verbs that sound like it are often intransitive too!
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading.

Lucky for you, the kanji readings for transitive and intransitive verbs are almost always the same. Once you learn one, you know them both! This reading is the same as 伝える.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
This one makes no sense (sorry!). When you <kanji>join</kanji> together with someone at a <kanji>metropolis</kanji>, you do it <vocabulary>at your convenience</vocabulary>. You're important, after all, so you just do what you want and make the other person wait in this giant metropolis while you move along leisurely. Imagine this, and keep thinking "at your convenience" as you walk about.

This word is usually used in a nicer way, though. As in, "do it at your convenience!"
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
The reading for 都 is an exception from what you learned with the kanji. To remember this, just think about someone who does something at their own convenience. They say, I'm going <reading>to go</reading> (つごう) where I want, when I want, at my own convenience.

The 合 (ごう) part is a reading you know from the kanji, though, so if you can get to "to go" with the mnemonic, you should be able to put two and two together to know that it's a long vowel ごう.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: You know that 映る is "to be reflected." Now you're doing the reflecting, which is really projecting (light). That's why this word is <vocabulary>to project</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as 映る. So long as you know the reading of 映る you should be able to read this one too.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: You hopefully remember that 要求 means "demand" . When you make that a verb, it becomes <vocabulary>to demand something</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading is just the vocab word 要求. It's also the regular on'yomi jukugo reading.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: What is something that will first <kanji>extinguish</kanji> something and then <kanji>change</kanji> it? One thing I can think of is your body. It takes in food, extinguishes it in your stomach, then changes it into things your body can use (and then excrete). That's why this "extinguish-change" process is your <vocabulary>digestion</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: This takes the <kanji>luck</kanji> meaning from the kanji. Think of it this way: If you're "carrying" you're going to create your own luck. Now nobody will mess with you, kanji gangstah. You carry guns and have a ton of <vocabulary>luck</vocabulary> because of it.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji! How... shall I say... <vocabulary>luck</vocabulary>-filled?

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb.

This is an intransitive verb. That means it does not take a direct object. Something comes off. Something is removed. No direct object here. That's why this verb means <vocabulary>to come off</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be removed</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading.

Lucky for you, the kanji readings for transitive and intransitive verbs are almost always the same. Once you learn one, you know them both! This reading is the same as 取る.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>energy</kanji> of the <kanji>warm</kanji>th will cause the <vocabulary>temperature</vocabulary> to go up and down. Energy goes up? Higher temperature because of more movement and activity. Energy goes down? Well, temperature gets colder and slower.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: This is <kanji>he</kanji> but plural. The "ra" makes it plural, making it "<vocabulary>they</vocabulary>" or "<vocabulary>them</vocabulary>." In modern Japanese, this word generally refers to a group of men or boys, but it can also be used for mixed groups as well.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: 誰 is <kanji>who</kanji>, 誰か is like asking "who?" If you don't know who it is, you just know it's <vocabulary>someone</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading comes from the reading you learned with the kanji.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
You're <kanji>tired</kanji> from <kanji>labor</kanji>. From this, you're showing <vocabulary>fatigue</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>weariness</vocabulary>.

疲労 is a little formal, so you might encounter it more often in writing than in conversation.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
You know that the kanji refers to a <kanji>floor</kanji> (as in the "fifth floor"). This word represents the version that comes after a number, shown with a 〜. Essentially, this has the same meaning as the kanji you learned, making it nice and easy.

Note that floor-counting systems can vary across different countries. In Japan the ground floor is generally called 一階, with the floors above being 二階, 三階, and so on.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji. Don't type in the 〜 or you'll get it wrong!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: A <kanji>metropolis</kanji> <kanji>city</kanji> is a <vocabulary>city</vocabulary>. When you're referring to just a plain ol' city, sans name, you can use this word.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: A <kanji>leaf</kanji> of the things you <kanji>say</kanji> is like a leaf from a tree of speaking. That leaf is a part of the whole language, it is a single <vocabulary>word</vocabulary>, though it can add up to be a <vocabulary>language</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>manner of speech</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
The reading for 言 is one you haven't learned, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

Now imagine that there are <vocabulary>word</vocabulary>s all over your <reading>coat</reading> (こと). It's completely covered in words. Which <vocabulary>language</vocabulary> are these words in? Why Japanese, of course! Think about which Japanese words you would want written on your coat.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well!
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This word uses the same reading as the one you learned with the kanji. <vocabulary> I</vocabulary> certainly like that and I bet you do too.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>earth</kanji> <kanji>sphere</kanji>! It's where we live and the planet we call home. It's <vocabulary>the earth</vocabulary>!
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: If you <kanji>meet</kanji> enough <kanji>member</kanji>s you will become a <vocabulary>member</vocabulary> yourself!
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: A <kanji>member</kanji> of a <kanji>boat</kanji> is called a <vocabulary>sailor</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: When <kanji>metropolis</kanji>es <kanji>meet</kanji> they become an <vocabulary>urban area</vocabulary>. This word is often used to mean <vocabulary>city</vocabulary> as opposed to the country or rural areas.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This has the same reading as the kanji you learned, meaning you know the reading!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: When you're talking or writing a paper, the part that <kanji>falls</kanji> at the end is the <vocabulary>conclusion</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned this reading already so you should be able to read it!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: A <kanji>period of time</kanji> <kanji>interval</kanji> is still a <vocabulary>period</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>interval</vocabulary> of time.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: When you <kanji>go</kanji> to <kanji>move</kanji> you're actually making an <vocabulary>action</vocabulary>. This word can also mean <vocabulary>behavior</vocabulary>, since your actions are what make up your behavior.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: This is the noun version of the kanji <kanji>gather</kanji>, so it means <vocabulary>gathering</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned this reading already so you should be able to read it!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>plant</kanji>, so the verb version is <vocabulary>to plant something</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to grow something</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
You haven't learned this reading for 植 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

You decided <vocabulary>to plant</vocabulary> an <reading>u</reading>ni (う) tree in your backyard. That's right, you can plant sea urchins and they'll grow like fruit off a really spiky tree. Just picture it. And then you'll get to eat all the uni you want!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
Who plays a <kanji>parent</kanji> <kanji>part</kanji> to you? Your <vocabulary>boss</vocabulary> or your <vocabulary>leader</vocabulary>!

親分 is an informal and sort of old-fashioned word for someone who's in charge of close-knit groups, like in gangs or traditional trades such as carpentry and fishing. The 親分 is like a parent figure who takes care of the other members.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This word consists of the kun'yomi reading for 親 and the on'yomi reading for 分. You've learned both of these so you should be able to read this already!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: Remember how you learned that 文字 can mean "characters?" Well make a <kanji>face</kanji> out of those characters and you've made a <vocabulary>kaomoji</vocabulary>! ʅ(◔౪◔ ) ʃ
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This word consists of the kun'yomi reading for 顔 added to the jukugo word 文字 that you already learned. You've learned these readings before, so reading this word should be nice and easy!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: A <kanji>club</kanji> <kanji>room</kanji> is a <vocabulary>clubroom</vocabulary>!
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: Remember how you learned that 大学院 means "graduate school" and 大学生 means "college student?" Well smush them together and you have a  <vocabulary>graduate student</vocabulary>!
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
This is a single kanji with no okurigana, so it's using the kun'yomi reading. You don't know this reading yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

You go down to the <vocabulary>harbor</vocabulary> and speak the secret password <reading>me natto</reading> (みなと) to buy some fresh natto. Imagine the salty air hitting your face as you whisper, "me natto." Now eat that yummy natto by the water! Mmmm!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
Remember how 文化 means "culture?" Well add <kanji>festival</kanji> to it and you end up with a <vocabulary>school festival</vocabulary> where students showcase a school's cultural activities!

文化祭 literally means a <vocabulary>culture festival</vocabulary>, but 文化 here means school culture — exhibits and productions related to the arts, science, and even food. 文化祭 are usually held in high schools and universities, where students take the lead in running them. Expect fun activities, classrooms turned into cafés or haunted houses, and lots of stage performances!
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You've learned all of these readings already, good for you!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This has the same reading as the kanji you learned, meaning you know the reading!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
The <kanji>lively</kanji> <kanji>move</kanji>s you make are your <vocabulary>activity</vocabulary>.

活動 includes all kinds of activities, including nature activities, club activities, economic activity, and so on!
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: Something you <kanji>wear</kanji>, and <kanji>wear</kanji> again, is something you <vocabulary>steadily</vocabulary> wear. You do it so often, it's reliable. Also, if you wear something this much it's steadily wearing away too.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This word uses on'yomi readings of the kanji you learned, twice. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. 

The kanji itself means <kanji>suffer</kanji>, and the verb is all about when you make someone else suffer. That's why it's <vocabulary>to hurt someone</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to torment</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to harass</vocabulary>.

You need to differentiate this from 苦しむ, which is about when YOU suffer. You can remember that 苦しめる is about making someone else suffer with this mnemonic: Who made you suffer? <reading>She ma</reading>de (しめ) me suffer! She's so mean!
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: By now, you've learned 苦しい and 苦しむ. The kanji in these words all use the same reading! Yay!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>finish</kanji>, so the verb version is <vocabulary>to finish something</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to end something</vocabulary>.

This is a transitive verb, meaning you finish something, like a long day at work!

You need to differentiate this from 終わる, which is when something just ends on its own. 終える is about when you make something end. Remember it like this: Canadians always end their sentences with "eh" え, right? Well that's how you know they're ending their sentence. Just listen for the "eh," eh?
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading, which you didn't learn with the kanji. Here's a mnemonic to help you:

You finally finished your school project. <reading>"Oh, A!"</reading> (おえ) you say to yourself, as though you can grade your own project.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
You <kanji>solve</kanji> a problem by working toward the <kanji>answer</kanji>. This is the act of <vocabulary>solving</vocabulary>, which eventually leads to the final <vocabulary>answer</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>solution</vocabulary>!

解答 specifically refers to solving problems and giving answers with a correct solution, often for structured contexts like exams or math problems. It can also refer to the answer or solution itself.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You learned the on'yomi for 答 with 回答, but here's a mnemonic for it in case you forgot:

The reward for <vocabulary>solving</vocabulary> this problem correctly is… A free trip to <reading>とう</reading>きょう! That's right, if you can work out the correct <vocabulary>solution</vocabulary> to this problem, you and a loved one will get an all-expenses-paid trip to とうきょう. Pretty cool, huh?

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
When you're doing a <kanji>water</kanji> <kanji>swim</kanji>, you're really just… well, <vocabulary>swimming</vocabulary>.

Note that 水泳 will usually refer to swimming as a sport or organized activity. When talking about swimming as a general action, 泳ぎ and 泳ぐ are more commonly used.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You've learned this reading for 水, but not for 泳, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

The only way you can <vocabulary>swim</vocabulary> is by chasing after <reading>a</reading>corns (えい). If somebody isn't dangling an acorn on a stick right in front of your face, you'd never get the motivation to swim. Good thing you're this into acorns.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
A <kanji>big</kanji> <kanji>west</kanji> <kanji>ocean</kanji>, you say? It's gotta be the <vocabulary>Atlantic Ocean</vocabulary>.

If you think about it from Japan's perspective, the Atlantic is a big, faraway ocean to the west, right?
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses on'yomi readings for all three kanji. You've seen these readings before, but the 西 reading (せい) is still pretty new, so here's a mnemonic refresher just in case:

While swimming in the <vocabulary>Atlantic Ocean</vocabulary>, you find a <reading>sa</reading>ber (せい). Yikes, how'd this rusty old saber get here? This thing must have floated across the Atlantic from some seaside battlefield of yore. Those old sabers are always washing up on Atlantic shores, you know.
